title: Driftwake
short_description: Carve a breaking wake through a field of wind-driven snow. Walk, sprint, jump and surf a dune plain under a low sun, bend water into five spells, and leave a trail the snow keeps for a minute — every pixel of it generated on the GPU at load, with no textures, meshes or animation clips anywhere in the build.
description:
Driftwake is an open field of wind-sculpted snow under a sun ten degrees above the horizon, and a figure to carve it with. The two things it is named for are the two things it is about: the drift — snow that is shaped by the wind and remembers everything you do to it — and the wake — a breaking wave of thrown powder that builds off your inside edge when you surf.

The ground is one static mesh drawn in a single call — eight nested rings whose every vertex is placed, morphed and displaced in the vertex shader, so nothing is rebuilt on the CPU and nothing is uploaded per frame. Underneath it, layered gradient noise with analytic derivatives builds broad transverse dune ridges, a long low swell, and drifts sheared along the prevailing wind so every lee face falls away asymmetrically. The snow itself carries baked macro slope, analytic sastrugi and ripples, three tiled scales of grain, and triplanar projection on the steep faces — over wrapped diffuse, a back-scatter subsurface term that turns shadowed hollows blue, and view-dependent glints that only fire at grazing angles.

Everywhere you step, the snow remembers. A persistent state buffer holds depression depth, displaced mass, compression and ice across an eighty-metre window that follows you without ever being copied. Feet leave trenches with raised berms rather than flat decals, and those berms break the silhouette and cast real shadows, because the displacement is geometry in the beauty pass and in all three shadow cascades alike. Trails slump, drift in from upwind and soften — about seventy percent of a trail's depth is still there a minute later. Jump and the landing punches a crater and throws powder; let the key go early and the rise is cut short.

Hold the right mouse and the walk becomes a carve. The wake is a swept mesh, not a particle trick: a breaking wave integrated from a turning tangent, so a single parameter runs it from a low heaped bank to a lip that hangs back across its own face, throwing nearly all the snow to the outside of the turn. Two populations of spray come off the same crest — a slow curtain that hugs it, and grains flung clear.

Five spells bend water over the field: a crescent of slush that ploughs a channel, a held ribbon drawing figure-eights that score lines into any snow it skims, a targeted eruption with a column that withdraws down its own axis, hexagonal ice grown along a golden-angle spiral, and three helices that lift the snow into the air around you. The water refracts without ever copying the scene — the sky model already knows what is below the horizon.

The sky is an atmosphere integral, not a captured photograph, so moving the sun drags the horizon warmth, the zenith gradient, the ambient tint and the shadow colour along with it. Every slider in the settings panel is live. The picture is entirely generated and the sound is mostly so: the wind bed that tracks the gusts, the hiss of a carve and the voice per spell are all synthesised live in Web Audio. The two sounds a microphone simply has are recordings — the boot breaking snow crust and the body landing in it — and the music is a track from the studio's own catalogue.

Four measured quality presets — performance, balanced, high and ultra — are in the menu, because this is a demanding frame and the bottom rung exists for machines that need it.
controls_keyboard: WASD move (camera-relative) · mouse look · click to capture the pointer · SHIFT sprint · wheel zoom · hold RIGHT MOUSE to snow-surf · SPACE jump · 1-5 cast the five spells (2 is a held cast) · F1 settings · F3 debug · Esc pause
